content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 2000 in Geneva under the Leprosy Elimination Monitoring (LEM) initiative. These guidelines provide a framework for monitoring and evaluating leprosy control programs. 2. In October 2005, C. Salisbury and colleagues published a study in Family Practice (Volume 22, Issue 5, Pages 560-569) that explored aspects of healthcare delivery and patient outcomes. 3. Erving Goffman, in his seminal 1963 work Stigma: Notes on the Management of Spoiled Identity, examined the social and psychological dimensions of stigma, including its impact on individuals with conditions such as leprosy. 4. A study published in Leprosy Review in 1972 (Volume 43, Issue 2, Pages 85-93) investigated the phenomenon of leprosy-related stigma within the continental United States, highlighting its social implications. 5. Jason Lillis, Jason B. Luoma, Michael E. Levin, and Steven C. Hayes developed the Weight Self-Stigma Questionnaire, a tool to measure self-stigma related to weight. This was published in Obesity in 2010 (Volume 18, Issue 5, Pages 971-976). 6. Richard Kravitz, in an article published in Journal of General Internal Medicine in April 1998 (Volume 13, Issue 4, Pages 280-282), discussed the significance of patient satisfaction in healthcare, questioning whether it is a critical outcome or a trivial pursuit. 7. Zemenchuk JK, Feightner JW, Hayward RA, Skarupski KA, and Katz SJ conducted a study on patients' desires and expectations for medical care in clinics in Michigan and Ontario. This was published in Journal of General Internal Medicine in 1998 (Volume 13, Issue 4, Pages 273-276). 8. Ware JE, Snyder MK, and Wright WR developed and validated scales to measure patient satisfaction with medical services. This work was documented in the NTIS publication (PB 288-329) in 1976. 9. The National Institute of Health and Family Welfare in New Delhi published field guidelines in 2004 for monitoring leprosy elimination in India. These guidelines provide practical instructions for field monitors. 10. The International Federation of Anti-Leprosy Associations (ILEP) and Netherlands Leprosy Relief (NLR) published guidelines in 2011 to reduce stigma associated with leprosy. These guidelines were developed in collaboration with stakeholders in London and Amsterdam. 11. The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy (2011-2015) by WHO aimed to reduce new cases of leprosy with grade-2 disabilities by 35% by the end of the strategy period. It emphasized early detection, quality care, and integrated service delivery. 12. Monitoring and evaluation are critical components of leprosy control programs. These processes rely on a minimum set of indicators to assess the impact, effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, and sustainability of services. 13. Routine data collection provides information on program progress and performance but may not adequately assess the quality of care. Additional indicators and methodologies have been identified to address this gap. 14. The document includes sample questionnaires for patient satisfaction surveys, community perceptions about leprosy, and perceived stigma. These tools are designed to gather feedback to improve leprosy services and reduce stigma. 15. The Enhanced Global Leprosy Strategy highlights the importance of monitoring and evaluation through before-and-after analyses to assess the effects of program interventions. It also incorporates additional indicators and methodologies to meet current needs.
